d: Steps 3 and 4: pick the right components to deep-dive, avoid rabbit holes, and close strong
goal: Your win today: choose and prioritise deep-dive topics with the interviewer, avoid low-signal rabbit holes, and deliver a wrap-up that names bottlenecks, failures, operations and the next scale step.
bookSections: Step 3: Design deep dive (with the news feed deep-dive figures); Step 4: Wrap up

stages.title: Where to Dig
stages.teaches: Step 3 budget: 10–25 minutes. By now you should have agreed goals and scope, a blueprint, feedback on it, and a sense of which areas to focus on. Work with the interviewer to identify and prioritise components. Interviewers differ: some (especially for senior roles) want high-level talk about performance characteristics, bottlenecks and resource estimates; most want you to dig into a few components. The book's examples: for a URL shortener, the hash function that turns a long URL into a short one; for a chat system, how to cut latency and how to support online/offline status.
stages.interaction: Match prompts to dives. Six prompt cards (URL shortener, chat system, news feed, rate limiter, unique ID generator, web crawler) and a tray of deep-dive topics (hash function for short codes; latency + online presence; fan-out and feed retrieval; the limiting algorithm such as token bucket; ID bit layout; politeness and de-duplication). Learner drags each topic to its prompt. Only the first two pairs are from this chapter; others are flagged 'preview of later chapters'. After matching, a 'priority' mini-step: for the news feed, order three candidate topics by importance: fan-out on publish (1), feed retrieval path (2), UI pagination style (3).
stages.check: Quiz: 'For a chat system, which deep-dive focus does the book suggest?' Options: Choosing a font / Reducing latency and supporting online/offline status (correct) / The company logo / Unit test layout.

stages.title: The Rabbit-Hole Trap
stages.sub: Spend minutes where the signal is
stages.teaches: Time management matters in step 3: don't spend it on details that don't show you can design scalable systems. The book's example: explaining Facebook's feed ranking formula (EdgeRank) in depth eats time without showing scalability skill. Design the most critical components first. Signal per minute is the metric to optimise.
stages.interaction: Deep-dive planner. A 20-minute deep-dive bar and 6 topic tiles, each showing a minute cost; signal value is hidden until chosen. Tiles: 'Fan-out on write vs read for 5,000 friends' (6 min, high), 'Feed retrieval: cache layers and hydrating post IDs' (5 min, high), 'Handling a celebrity with millions of followers' (4 min, high), 'EdgeRank formula in detail' (8 min, low: trap), 'Which JSON library to use' (3 min, none), 'Media upload via object storage + CDN' (4 min, medium). Learner fills the bar; then 'Run the dive' animates a signal meter as each tile plays. Max score: the three high tiles plus media (19 min). Picking EdgeRank shows the interviewer glancing at the clock and a toast: 'interesting, but how does this scale?'
stages.check: Quiz: 'Why is a long EdgeRank explanation a poor use of deep-dive time?' Options: It's a secret / It shows little about scalable design while burning minutes (correct) / Ranking is never discussed in interviews / Interviewers don't know what it is.

stages.title: Peek at the Feed Deep Dive
stages.sub: A preview of fan-out (built in Ch. 11)
stages.teaches: The chapter's deep-dive figures expand the two flows: publishing (web servers, post service, fanout service, notification service, plus caches and DBs) and retrieval (news feed service reading feed cache then fetching post and user details). The key idea to preview: fan-out on write (push: when Alice posts, write her post ID into each friend's precomputed feed, fast reads, expensive for users with huge follower counts) vs fan-out on read (pull: build the feed when someone opens it, cheap writes, slower reads). With up to 5,000 friends, one post means up to 5,000 cache writes on push. Full treatment, including the hybrid used for celebrities, is in Chapter 11.
stages.interaction: Predict-then-watch slider. A friend-count slider (10 → 5,000 → 'celebrity: 10M followers') and a toggle Push / Pull. The learner predicts, for each combo, whether the publish or the read will be slow (two buttons). Then animate: push with 5,000 friends shows 5,000 tiny writes streaming into feed-cache cells (fast publish counter at ~5,000 writes, instant read); push with 10M shows the write counter running for a long time with a 'hot key / backlog' warning; pull shows the publish as one write, and Bob's read pulling from many friends' post lists (read latency bar grows with friend count). Correct predictions: push → slow publish for celebrities, fast reads; pull → fast publish, slow reads.
stages.check: Quiz: 'With fan-out on write, which user makes publishing expensive?' Options: A user with 3 friends / A user with millions of followers (correct) / A user who never posts / A user on mobile.

stages.title: Land the Plane
stages.teaches: Step 4 budget: 3–5 minutes. The interviewer may ask follow-ups or let you choose what to add. Directions the book suggests: point out bottlenecks and possible improvements (never claim the design is perfect; there's always something to improve, and this shows critical thinking); give a short recap, especially if you discussed several options; error cases such as a server failing or network loss; operations: how you'd monitor metrics and error logs and roll the system out; the next scale step, e.g., what changes going from 1 million to 10 million users; other refinements you'd make with more time. And remember: the interview isn't over until the interviewer says it is.
stages.interaction: Closing-move picker. Timer shows 4:00 left. Eight closing cards; learner must pick exactly 3, then press 'Deliver'. Strong cards: 'Name the bottleneck: fan-out for celebrity accounts; propose a hybrid', 'What happens if the feed cache cluster loses a node: rebuild from the post DB and fall back to pull', 'How I'd monitor it: feed load latency, fan-out queue depth, error rates; roll out behind a flag', 'What breaks at 10× users: shard the post DB, add cache tiers'. Weak/trap cards: 'Say: I think the design is basically perfect', 'Re-explain every box from the start in detail', 'Ask: so... are we done?', 'Start a brand-new design for search'. Scoring: 3 strong = full XP; recap card is counted strong only if multiple options were discussed (show this rule in the reveal). Each trap picked costs a heart and shows why.
stages.check: Quiz: 'Interviewer: anything you'd improve?' Options: No, it's complete / Yes: the fan-out bottleneck for celebrities, plus monitoring and a plan for 10× growth (correct) / I'd rewrite it in another language / I'd need to check the book.

stages.title: Boss: Steps 3 & 4 Gauntlet
stages.sub: Dig, don't drown; close, don't coast
stages.teaches: Mixed decisions from the second half of the interview.
stages.interaction: Q.boss() with fixed choices: 'Go deeper here', 'Zoom out / move on', 'Ask the interviewer', 'Name a weakness'. Scenarios (answer, why): 1) Minute 24, you're 6 minutes into tuning a JSON parser → Zoom out / move on (low signal). 2) Interviewer: 'Tell me more about how fan-out handles celebrities.' → Go deeper here (they've signalled their priority). 3) You see two equally reasonable deep-dive targets and don't know which they care about → Ask the interviewer. 4) Minute 41, interviewer: 'Anything else?' → Name a weakness (bottleneck + improvement). 5) You've been explaining the ranking formula for 7 minutes → Zoom out / move on (rabbit hole). 6) Interviewer: 'What if a feed cache node dies?' → Go deeper here (failure handling is classic signal). 7) Wrap-up: you've covered fan-out but not operations → Name a weakness (say what you'd monitor and what's still fragile). Name: '🕳️ The Rabbit King'.
stages.check: Pass with at most 2 wrong; outro: 'Go deep where the interviewer points, name your weak spots before they do.'

stages.title: Say It Like a Senior
stages.teaches: A strong close is structured: weakness, failure, operations, next scale step.
stages.interaction: Q.drill(): prompt 'Four minutes left. The interviewer says: "Anything you'd add?"' Model answer (our words): 'A few things. The biggest bottleneck is fan-out for accounts with huge followings; I'd switch those to pull-on-read and keep push for everyone else. If a feed cache node fails, feeds can be rebuilt from the post store, with a pull-based fallback meanwhile. Operationally, I'd watch feed load latency, fan-out queue depth and error rates, and roll changes out gradually. At ten times the users I'd shard the post database and add more cache tiers. With more time I'd look at ranking and spam filtering.'
stages.check: Self-grade checks: I named a bottleneck and a fix · I covered a failure case · I mentioned monitoring or rollout · I said what changes at the next scale step.

caveats: EdgeRank was Facebook's early, publicly described ranking formula; Facebook moved to machine-learned ranking years ago. The book uses it only as an example of a low-signal rabbit hole.
The push/pull fan-out comparison here is a preview; Chapter 11 covers it properly, including the hybrid approach and cache tiers.
Some interviewers deliberately steer the deep dive into areas you didn't plan; following their lead beats sticking to your plan.
